activities.anchor: Statistical mechanics is where those rules come
activities.caption: pair each counting term with its meaning
activities.name: smCountMatch

config.prompt: The conceptual leap — pair each piece with its work:

pairs.right: one microscopic arrangement of all ~10²³ molecules
the big-picture description — same pressure, same temperature
whichever macrostate has the most microstates — a bias the numbers make effectively absolute

config.why: The laws of heat are not new forces but the statistics of ordinary mechanics applied to astronomical numbers of particles.

activities.anchor: Start with the smallest example that shows the avalanche
activities.caption: build the coin-flip avalanche, step by step
activities.name: smCoinsOrder

config.prompt: Assemble the counting argument that becomes the second law:
items: Flip 10 coins: the macrostate '5 heads' has W = C(10,5) = 252 microstates; '10 heads' has exactly 1
Flip 100 coins: '50 heads' has W ≈ 1.0 × 10²⁹ microstates versus 1 for 'all heads'
The distribution's width only grows like √N, so the relative fluctuations shrink
Scale to 10²³ molecules: the most-probable macrostate outnumbers any near-miss by factors like 10^(10²¹)
Boltzmann's insight: entropy IS this count — S = k·ln W, carved on his gravestone in Vienna
config.why: The logarithm makes entropy additive — combine two systems and the microstates multiply, W = W₁·W₂, so entropies add.

activities.caption: find the faulty line in this student's entropy notes
activities.name: smEntropySpot

config.prompt: One line of this student's entropy notes is wrong — click it:
lines: Entropy counts microstates per macrostate — not everyday 'messiness'.
A crystal at absolute zero and a tidy room are both low-entropy in their everyday senses.
Tidying a room lowers the universe's total entropy, so tidy rooms violate the second law.
Cleaning exports more entropy — heat, sweat, discarded packaging — than it removes.
Physicists increasingly prefer 'spread': how spread-out energy and matter are over available microstates.
config.correction: The room's surroundings pay with interest: the entropy exported exceeds the local tidy-up, so no violation — the second law is bookkeeping, not a ban on order.
config.why: 'Disorder' is a poor gloss; the thermodynamic quantity is a count, and 'spread' is the preferred reading.

config.root: Feed energy into a system whose entropy falls with energy — a population-inverted laser medium. Walk the temperature ladder.

start.text: The statistical definition says 1/T = ΔS/ΔE. What is this system's temperature?

wrongturn.text: It can — in population-inverted systems, and the definition then gives a negative absolute temperature, consistent arithmetic and all.

choices.label: Now touch it to ordinary matter

contact.text: Put it in contact with any positive-temperature body. Which way does energy flow?

inflow.text: That flow shrinks the universe's W — the inverted system is hotter than infinity, so the ledger runs the other way.

outflow.text: Energy flows out: the negative-temperature system heats every ordinary body it touches. The definition earns its keep.

config.why: Temperature is the entropy price of an added joule — follow 1/T = ΔS/ΔE honestly and negative absolute temperatures sit past infinity on the ladder.

activities.anchor: temperature measures how much heat a body contains
activities.caption: drag the divider — the 90 °C cup vs the 30 °C bath
activities.name: smBathCompare

config.prompt: Which holds more thermal energy — and what does the thermometer actually read?

before.label: a cup of 90 °C tea
before.text: Energy-dense but small. Temperature is the intensity — the entropy price of each added joule (1/T = ΔS/ΔE), not the amount of energy aboard. The tea's energy dumps itself eagerly into the bath.

after.label: a bathtub of 30 °C water
after.text: Energy content scales with mass: the bath holds hundreds of times more thermal energy than the cup — colder, yet vastly richer in energy.

config.why: A hot small body is energy-dense but entropy-poor per joule — exactly the distinction 1/T = ΔS/ΔE encodes.

activities.caption: place the marker where pressure has halved
activities.name: smScaleHeightPlace

config.prompt: The barometric formula P(h) = P₀·e^(−mgh/kT) is the Boltzmann factor with E = mgh. For air at 288 K, pressure halves roughly every 6 km. Place the marker at that half-pressure altitude:
config.why: The scale height mgh/kT ≈ 8.5 km — and with the halving every ~6 km, this is why airliners pressurise and Everest demands bottled oxygen.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — equipartition and the freeze-out
activities.name: smEquipCloze

config.text: In thermal equilibrium, every quadratic degree of freedom carries %%0%% on average. A monatomic gas (three translational degrees) therefore has heat capacity (3/2)R ≈ %%1%% J/(mol·K) — exactly what helium shows; diatomic nitrogen adds two rotational degrees for (5/2)R ≈ 20.8. But add vibration and the data show it %%2%% out below ~1000 K — classical physics over-promising, quantum mechanics asserting itself.
config.hint: One share per degree of freedom; a number near 12; a word for what cold does to vibration.

activities.caption: which curve is the Maxwell–Boltzmann speed distribution?
activities.name: smMBTrace

config.prompt: A gas in thermal equilibrium — which curve is the distribution of molecular speeds?

curves.label: a bare Boltzmann factor — no v² factor
v² alone — growth without the exponential cutoff

config.xlabel: molecular speed (in units where the peak ≈ 1)
config.why: The shape matters more than the peak: a long, thin tail, and the tail does the chemistry — evaporation, reaction rates, and which atmospheres a planet keeps.
